questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Despite what the critics say, the
director is thinking that his latest
movie will be a blockbuster.
No Error
options_hi: Despite what the critics say, the
director is thinking that his latest
movie will be a blockbuster.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “is thinking” with “thinks”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Stative Verbs -

These verbs describe a state, opinion, or condition (e.g., think, believe, know, understand, own, possess).

They are generally not used in the Continuous (Progressive) tense because they represent a permanent or semi-permanent fact rather than a temporary action.

The "Think" Nuance: 1. When think means "to have an opinion" (a state), use Simple Present.

2. When think means "to deliberate or use the brain for an activity" (an action), you may use Continuous.

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the director isn't performing the physical act of "using his brain" at a specific moment; rather, he holds the opinion or believes that his movie will be successful. Since "think" here represents a mental state or belief, it must be in the Simple Present tense (thinks). Using "is thinking" makes it sound like a temporary physical process, which is grammatically incorrect for expressing an opinion.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 ✅: I think you are a genius. (Opinion - Stative). Example 2 ✅: I am thinking about moving to London. (Planning/Mental process)

Example 3 ✅: This house belongs to my uncle. (Possession - Stative; never "is belonging")

REMEMBER THE LIST of Stative verbs:- Think, Believe, Consider, Have, Own, Possess, Look, Seem, Appear, Consist, Contain, Comprise, Feel, Smell, Taste, Sound, Know, Resemble, Like, Love, Want, Agree, Hate, Forgive, Forget, Remember, Depend, Exist etc.

questions.q_en:
In the sentence below, identify the type of adverb of the word “carefully”:

The scientist carefully examined the data before presenting the final conclusions to the research committee.
questions.q_hi:
In the sentence below, identify the type of adverb of the word “carefully”:

The scientist carefully examined the data before presenting the final conclusions to the research committee.
options_en: Adverb of Time
Adverb of Place
Adverb of Manner
Adverb of Degree
questions.solution_en:
Answer: C) Adverb of Manner

Explanation: An adverb of manner tells us how an action is performed.

Here, “carefully” modifies the verb “examined.”

examined how? → carefully

Since it describes the manner in which the scientist examined the data, it is an adverb of manner.

had it

had it
didn’t it

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) - “had it”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Negative Word + Inversion Structure

  • Words like hardly, scarcely, rarely, seldom make a sentence negative in meaning.

  • When the statement is negative in meaning, the tag must be positive.

  • Also, the auxiliary used in the inverted structure must be repeated.

💢 Application to the Given Question - “Hardly” makes the sentence negative in meaning.

The auxiliary used is had. So, the tag must be had it? (positive).

❌ Not: “hadn’t it?” because that would create double negativity.

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ - Scarcely had the meeting begun, had it?

Example 2 ✅ - Rarely does he question authority, does he?

No Error
options_hi: The environmentalists expressed grave concern that Nile,
which has been the lifeblood of Egypt for millennia, is facing

questions.solution_en:
Replace “Nile” with “the Nile”.

Rule / Concept: Use of 'The' with Geographical Entities –

The definite article 'the' must be used before the names of specific geographical features such as oceans (The Pacific), seas (The Red Sea), rivers (The Amazon), deserts (The Gobi), and mountain ranges (The Alps). These are unique, large-scale natural entities, and 'the' is used to provide the necessary definiteness to their proper names.

Corrected Sentence- The environmentalists expressed grave concern that the Nile, which has been the lifeblood of Egypt for millennia, is facing unprecedented levels of pollution due to rapid industrialization.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips-

Ranges vs. Peaks: This is the biggest trap. Use 'the' for ranges (The Himalayas, The Rockies) but NEVER use 'the' for individual peaks (Mount Everest, K2, Annapurna).

The "Specific" River: Even if the word "River" isn't written (e.g., "The Nile" instead of "The Nile River"), the article 'the' remains mandatory.

📌 Rule / Concept: “It” Structure in Reporting Verb Passive

When the active structure is:

Subject (They/People) + reporting verb (say, believe, think, report, expect, consider, etc.) + that-clause

One correct passive transformation is:

It + be (in correct tense) + V³ + that-clause

This structure is preferred when the focus is on the reported information rather than the subject performing the reporting. It maintains the tense of the verb inside the “that-clause.”

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

Use “It + be + V³ + that-clause” for reporting verb passives.

Do not mix this with the infinitive structure unless converting differently.

Maintain the tense inside the that-clause.

When expressions like it is necessary that, it is essential that, it is important that are followed by a clause, the verb in that-clause takes the base form (subjunctive mood). In passive construction, the structure becomes: It + is + adjective + that + object + be + V³. The word “be” is used instead of “is/are” because the clause remains in the subjunctive form.

📌 Application to the Given Question

It is necessary that the regulatory body implement the new KYC norms immediately. Here, “implement” is in the subjunctive base form (not “implements”). In passive voice, “the new KYC norms” becomes the subject of the that-clause. Since the sentence is mandative/subjunctive, we use “be implemented” (not “are implemented”). Hence, “It is necessary that the new KYC norms be implemented immediately” is the correct transformation. Option (A) incorrectly uses the indicative “are implemented.” Options (C) and (D) distort the structure and meaning.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

After expressions of necessity, demand, suggestion, use the base verb (subjunctive). In passive subjunctive, use “be + V³,” not “is/are.” Do not shift to the indicative mood. Preserve the original structure carefully.

📌 Rule / Concept: Narrative Tense Consistency

When a sentence describes a specific event that occurred in the past, all the main verbs related to that event must remain in the Simple Past Tense .

If a sentence provides a time-marker in the past (such as "when... arrived"), it establishes a "Past Zone."

💢 Application to the Given Question

"...Dr. Mehta take charge... when multiple accident victims arrived..."

There are two related actions in this sentence:

  1. The victims arrived (Simple Past - $V_2$).

  2. Dr. Mehta take charge (Simple Present - $V_1$).

The word "when" creates a direct temporal link between the two actions. Since the arrival of the victims happened in the past, the act of taking charge must also have happened at that same past moment. Therefore, "take" (Present) must be changed to "took" (Past) to match the narrative context.

Corrected Sentence

Celebrated as one of the most dedicated surgeons in the hospital, Dr. Mehta took charge of the emergency unit when multiple accident victims arrived late at night.

Rule / Concept: Pluralizing Compound Nouns (Noun-Main vs. Phrasal Nouns)

The rule for pluralizing compound nouns depends on how the compound is structured:

-Noun + Preposition/Adverb (Noun is the Head): If there is a clear "principal" or "main" noun, you add the 's' to that noun.

-Example: Passers-by, Runners-up, Mothers-in-law.

-Verb + Preposition/Adverb (Phrasal Nouns): If the compound noun is formed from a phrasal verb and has no clear internal noun, the 's' is added at the very end.

Example: Break-ins, Check-outs, Take-offs, Write-ups

Application to the Given Question

The term "break-in" comes from the phrasal verb "to break in." In this compound form, "break" is not acting as a standalone noun being modified; rather, the entire phrase "break-in" functions as a single noun meaning a burglary. Therefore, to make it plural, the 's' must be placed at the end of the entire unit. "Breaks-in" is a common error made by over-applying the rule for words like "passers-by."

Corrected Sentence - In response to the recent surge in daring break-ins across the gated community, the local police department has increased its nocturnal patrols.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 - The pilot managed three successful take-offs during the training session.

Example 2 - We observed several passers-by helping the stray dog. (Here, 'passer' is the main noun).

Example 3 - There were multiple check-outs happening simultaneously at the hotel lobby.

📌 Rule / Concept: Collocations (Verb + Noun Pairing) -

In English, certain nouns "belong" to specific verbs. These fixed pairs are called collocations. Using the wrong verb with a noun is a common error tested in high-level exams like SSC CGL Mains.

Make is used for decisions, choices, plans, and arrangements (creating something that didn't exist before).

Take is used for actions, risks, exams, or physical objects.

💢 Application to the Given Question - The word "choice" refers to a mental decision-making process. In standard English, we "make a choice", just as we "make a decision." Using "take" is a literal translation error from other languages but is grammatically incorrect in English. Even with the adjective "cautious" in between, the core verb-noun relationship must remain "make... choice."

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

The "Decision" Rule: If you can replace the word "choice" with "decision," you should almost always use the verb Make.

Common "Make" Pairings: Make a mistake, make a phone call, make a noise, make a promise.

Common "Take" Pairings: Take a chance, take a seat, take an exam, take a look.

questions.q_en: If the revised protocol ______ approved by the ethics committee, the study will proceed to the data-collection phase.
questions.q_hi: If the revised protocol ______ approved by the ethics committee, the study will proceed to the data-collection phase.
options_en:

Had been

Would be
options_hi:
is

were

Had been

Would be
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

👉 Replace “_____” with “is”.

📌 Rule / Concept: First Conditional (Real / Possible Future Condition)

The First Conditional is used to talk about real, possible, and achievable situations in the present or future and their likely results.

Standard Structure:

If + Present Simple → will + base verb

Key point:

 

  • The if-clause states a real condition, not a hypothetical or unreal one.
  • Therefore, it must use a present tense, not a past or modal form.

💢 Application to the Given Question

“If the revised protocol _____ approved by the ethics committee, the study will proceed to the data-collection phase.”

Here:

 

  • Approval by the ethics committee is a real and pending possibility.
  • The result (the study will proceed) is a future action dependent on that approval.

Because the condition is real and open, the correct verb in the if-clause is present simple:

  • “is approved” → grammatically and logically correct.

Why the others fail:

  • were → marks an unreal or hypothetical condition (Second Conditional), which is not intended.
  • had been → shifts the sentence to an unreal past (Third Conditional), which contradicts the future result.
  • would be → modals are not used in the if-clause of standard conditionals.
